concept.name: Secondary market
concept.definition: The market in which previously issued securities are traded among investors, without the issuer receiving the proceeds. Secondary trading provides the liquidity and continuous pricing that make primary issuance possible.
concept.intuition: This is the resale market: investors trade existing shares with each other, and the company is not a party to the deal.
concept.mechanics: Investors route orders to exchanges, alternative trading systems, or OTC dealers; the resulting transaction prices disseminate through market data feeds and become the reference for valuations, index levels, and new issuance pricing.
concept.failure_modes: Secondary liquidity can be one-sided or illusory in stress — quotes widen or vanish exactly when investors most want to sell, and prices can gap away from fundamentals during panics.
concept.misconceptions: Everyday buying and selling of stock does not fund the company; only primary-market purchases do. A high secondary price also does not by itself mean the issuer is financially healthy.
concept.example: An investor sells 500 shares of Apple on Nasdaq to another investor; Apple Inc. receives nothing from this secondary-market trade.

citations.source: SEC, Concept Release on Equity Market Structure (Release No. 34-61358)
citations.section: Section I (the secondary market for U.S.-listed equities)
